title: Ranveer Singh Has ₹1,800 Crore, a Lawsuit, and a Zombie Apocalypse — All at the Same Time
excerpt: Dhurandhar 2 completes a historic 100-day run while the Don 3 fallout rages on and a ₹300-crore post-apocalyptic thriller quietly fires up in the background
body:
There is no one in Bollywood right now living a wilder chapter than Ranveer Singh.

On one hand, the man just completed a milestone most actors can only fantasize about. Dhurandhar 2: The Revenge — the Aditya Dhar-directed spy actioner that turned him into a genuine crossover phenomenon — hit 100 days in theatres on June 26, with a worldwide gross north of ₹1,800 crore. That's not a number. That's a statement. It's the kind of theatrical run that forces an industry obsessed with opening weekends to sit down and rethink everything it thought it knew about audience behaviour.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=xtamgtzZTT0

And the diaspora was a massive part of this. Dhurandhar 2 overtook Pathaan to become the biggest Indian grosser in the United Kingdom, and shattered Baahubali 2's record for the biggest second Friday in North America for an Indian film. If you're an NRI and you somehow missed the theatrical experience — it finally hit JioHotstar on June 4. You've run out of excuses.

But here's the thing about being Bollywood's biggest star in 2026: it apparently comes with a side order of industry warfare.

The Don 3 Fallout

> "His official statement spoke of "dignity, maturity and mutual respect." Then he hit back where it counts — with a formal legal notice to FWICE, challenging the directive's legality."

Ranveer's exit from Don 3 — the long-gestating sequel that was supposed to continue the legacy of Amitabh Bachchan and Shah Rukh Khan — has turned into one of the ugliest backstage dramas the industry has seen in years. According to reports, Ranveer grew dissatisfied with the script and walked away. Excel Entertainment — Farhan Akhtar and Ritesh Sidhwani's production house — claims to have spent approximately ₹45 crore on pre-production and wants compensation.

> "Ranveer kept asking for changes and didn't like what the final draft read. Excel claims they went ahead with pre-production only after Singh gave his go-ahead." — Variety India

![Aditya Dhar — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9d/Aditya_Dhar_at_IFFI_2019_%28cropped%29.jpg)

What followed was an escalation nobody expected. The Federation of Western India Cine Employees (FWICE) issued a non-cooperation directive against Ranveer — not quite a ban (they don't have that power, as they later clarified), but a public call for their affiliated workers and technicians to refuse to work with him. The move split the industry. Producer Nikhil Dwivedi questioned whether contractual disputes should become livelihood threats. Veteran producer T.P. Aggarwal challenged FWICE in court. Even Kangana Ranaut stood up for him.

Ranveer, for his part, played it cool in public. His official statement spoke of "dignity, maturity and mutual respect." Then he hit back where it counts — with a formal legal notice to FWICE, challenging the directive's legality. As of now, the courts will decide.

But the thing about Ranveer Singh is that he never stops working, even when the industry is trying to figure out how to feel about him.

Pralay: The ₹300-Crore Zombie Bet

On June 24 — paparazzi caught Ranveer leaving Hansal Mehta's office in Mumbai in an all-black ensemble, face hidden behind a mask and dark glasses. Casting director Mukesh Chhabra was there too. The mission: Pralay, a ₹300-crore post-apocalyptic zombie survival thriller set to begin shooting in August 2026.

Directed by Jai Mehta — Hansal's son, the man behind *Lootere* and co-director of *Scam 1992* — Pralay is being described as a dystopian spectacle unlike anything Indian cinema has attempted. South Indian star Kalyani Priyadarshan, fresh off the blockbuster *Lokah*, has been locked for her Bollywood debut opposite Ranveer. The production plans to merge physical sets with AI-driven visuals to build a world that exists nowhere else on screen.

Ranveer is also producing, through his new banner Maa Kasam Films. It's his costliest solo venture ever, a genre Bollywood has barely touched, and he's doing it while technically under an industry non-cooperation order that he's fighting in court.

That, more than any box office number, tells you everything about where his head is. The ₹1,800 crore is validation. The Don 3 drama is noise. Pralay is the bet — the kind of swing-for-the-fences move that either creates a new template or crashes spectacularly. Either way, nobody's looking away.

For the diaspora, the timing is perfect. Dhurandhar 2 is streaming on JioHotstar for anyone who missed the theatrical run. And Pralay — if it delivers on its promise — could land as early as late 2027. By then, we'll know whether the FWICE standoff is a footnote or a turning point.

Right now, Ranveer Singh is simultaneously the most celebrated and the most controversial star in Indian cinema. It's messy, it's dramatic, and it's compulsively watchable — which, come to think of it, is exactly the kind of movie he'd want to be in.
